lesson.title: Same Subjects, Two Measurements: Recognizing Paired Data
lesson.summary: Paired data arises when each observation in one set has a natural partner in the other, such as before-and-after measurements on the same subject; the right move is to collapse the two columns into one column of differences.
lesson.body:
Not every comparison of two sets of numbers involves two independent samples. Recall from matched pairs design that a study can link observations together on purpose: measuring the same subject twice, once before and once after a treatment, or deliberately matching two different subjects on some trait, like age or severity of illness, before giving them different treatments. Twins, siblings, and before-and-after measurements on one person are the classic examples. Whenever that kind of natural, non-arbitrary link exists between an observation in group 1 and one specific observation in group 2, the data are called paired, or matched pairs.

The key move with paired data is a structural one, not just a labeling choice. Instead of treating the data as two separate samples of size n1 and n2, you compute one difference per pair, d equals measurement 1 minus measurement 2, and end up with a single list of n differences. That single list is then analyzed exactly like any other one-sample quantitative data set: it has a sample mean, xbar_d (recall sample mean), and a sample standard deviation, s_d, describing how much the differences themselves vary from pair to pair.

Here is a concrete example. Six participants in an 8-week weight loss program are weighed before and after. 
Participant 1: before 180, after 176, difference 4.
Participant 2: before 165, after 162, difference 3.
Participant 3: before 200, after 193, difference 7.
Participant 4: before 210, after 208, difference 2.
Participant 5: before 190, after 183, difference 7.
Participant 6: before 175, after 171, difference 4.
Adding the six differences: 4 plus 3 plus 7 plus 2 plus 7 plus 4 equals 27, so xbar_d equals 27 divided by 6, or 4.5. To find s_d, take each difference's deviation from 4.5, square it, and add: (4 minus 4.5) squared is 0.25, (3 minus 4.5) squared is 2.25, (7 minus 4.5) squared is 6.25, (2 minus 4.5) squared is 6.25, (7 minus 4.5) squared is 6.25, and (4 minus 4.5) squared is 0.25. These sum to 21.5. Dividing by n minus 1, which is 5, gives a variance of 4.3, and taking the square root gives s_d of about 2.074.

Why bother collapsing to differences at all, instead of just comparing the before-group average to the after-group average directly? Because the two measurements within a pair are usually correlated. A participant who starts heavier tends to still weigh more than average after the program, even if the program worked. That shared, person-specific variation is not something we care about, what we care about is how much each person changed. Subtracting within each pair cancels out that shared variation before any analysis happens, leaving behind only the variability in the change itself. That is exactly the raw material the paired t-test, up next, needs, and skipping this step is exactly the mistake examined closely in when to pair.
